title: Judge the call, not the luck
principle: Judge a call by what you knew then, not the result.

screens.text: Let me start with a cricket story. It's the 2007 T20 World Cup final against Pakistan. Pakistan need 13 runs from the last over, with one wicket left. Harbhajan was the usual choice, but he gave away three sixes in his last over. So Dhoni picks Joginder Sharma.

screens.prompt: Joginder had played very few games for India. Before I tell you what happened, do you think Dhoni made a good choice?

options.label: A sensible choice with the options he had
Can't tell until we see the result

screens.why: Here's what happened. The first ball was a wide. Misbah missed the next ball, then hit a full toss for six. With six needed from four balls, Misbah tried a scoop shot. Sreesanth caught it. India won by five runs, and Dhoni's choice became famous.

screens.prompt: Now imagine Misbah's scoop had gone for four, and Pakistan had won. Would that make Dhoni's call any worse?
screens.why: Exactly. Dhoni chose before the over began, and he knew the same things in both stories. Only the result of one ball changed. Newspapers would have called it a bad choice, but they would be judging the result, not Dhoni's thinking.

wrong.a: I see what you did: you judged the call by the final score. But Dhoni chose before the over began, and nothing he knew then had changed. Only where one ball landed was different.
wrong.c: I can see why you chose the middle answer. But luck cannot make a choice worse after it is made. Dhoni knew the same things either way, so it was the same choice.

screens.title: Resulting
screens.text: Calling it a bad choice would be a mistake. Imagine two students. One copies and gets full marks. Another understands but makes one mistake. Marks alone do not show who made the better choice. Poker player Annie Duke calls this mistake resulting: judging a decision only by what happened.

screens.prompt: Let's go back to that final. I'll show you five things. For each one, tell me: did Dhoni know it when he chose?

items.text: Harbhajan had gone for three sixes
The first ball would be a wide
Joginder had bowled the last over in the semi-final
India would win by five runs

screens.why: Exactly. Start with what Dhoni knew when he chose. The wide, the scoop and the final score all came later. They tell you what happened, but they can't change how good his thinking was.

screens.title: From their story to yours
screens.text: Dhoni made one big choice in front of millions. You will make many smaller choices, and some good ones will still go wrong. You must not learn the wrong lesson from them. Imagine you run a lunch tiffin service for offices. Let's test your judgement.

screens.prompt: A fair stall costs ₹10,000. 1 time in 4, you get an order that leaves you ₹60,000. On average, what do you make per fair?
screens.why: Well done. ₹60,000 spread across four fairs is ₹15,000 per fair on average. Each fair costs ₹10,000, so you make ₹5,000 per fair on average. It is a good choice even though most fairs bring no order.

wrong.a: I see what you did: ₹60,000 minus the ₹10,000 stall. But you win that ₹60,000 only 1 time in 4. Spread it across four fairs, that's ₹15,000 each, then take off the ₹10,000: ₹5,000.
wrong.c: That's what you lose at one fair with no order, and most fairs will have no order. But ₹60,000 ÷ 4 is ₹15,000 per fair on average. Take away ₹10,000, and you get ₹5,000.

screens.prompt: You go to two fairs and get no order at either. Your partner says, "Fairs don't work. Let's stop." What do you say?

options.label: Agree. Two empty fairs prove it
Try a bigger, costlier fair next
Not yet. Two empty fairs are normal

screens.why: Exactly. A fair gets an order only 1 time in 4, so most fairs bring nothing, and two empty fairs in a row happen more often than not. Judge the fairs after many tries, not two. Over time, each fair still makes you ₹5,000 on average.

wrong.a: I see why: two empty fairs feel like proof. But a fair gets an order only 1 time in 4, so two empty fairs in a row happen more often than not. Judge it after many fairs, not two.
wrong.c: That changes the bet before you know if it works. A fair gets an order only 1 time in 4, so two empty fairs are normal. Keep going, and judge it after many fairs.

screens.prompt: Now the other way round. You hired a cook without a trial day, and that month was your best ever. What's the lesson?

options.label: Keep the cook, but give the next one a trial
Skip trials from now on. It worked
The cook earned you that whole month

screens.why: Right. The good month doesn't prove that skipping the trial was smart, because the cook might have helped, or a festival, or a big new client. Keep the cook if they're good, but don't let one lucky month teach you a careless way to hire.

wrong.b: I see what you did: the month went well, so the method must be fine. That's resulting the other way round. You skipped the check and got lucky, so give the next cook a trial day.
wrong.c: Maybe, but a festival or a new office client could explain that month too. You can't tell from the result alone, so keep the cook if they're good, and give the next one a trial day.

screens.prompt: When a big call goes wrong, here's how to review it fairly. Put the steps in order.
steps: Write down what you knew then
Write down what you chose, and why
Ask: was it the thinking, or the luck?
Change your method only if the thinking was wrong
screens.why: Well done. First, look at the decision using only what you knew at that time. Then look at the result and ask what it teaches you. We did the same with Dhoni: first what he knew, then what happened.

screens.setup: Then one of your calls goes wrong. Before taking a new office client, you checked carefully: three good references and five years in business. Two months later it shuts down, owing you ₹36,000, and your partner says, 'No more new clients. Ever.'
screens.question: Was it a bad call, and what do you do now?

options.label: Agree. Only old clients from now on
options.outcome: You're safe for a while. Then two old offices move away, and with no new clients coming in, your kitchen runs half empty.
options.why: One bad result made you stop using a good method. That's resulting. You would also stop taking good new clients.
options.better: Keep checking new clients, and ask them for the first month in advance.

options.label: Keep the checks, and ask new clients for a month's advance
options.outcome: New offices keep signing up. Each one pays its first month up front, so if one shuts down, you lose far less.
options.why: Well played. One failed client doesn't prove your checks were bad, so you keep them. But the loss showed one risk you can reduce: how much a new client can owe you before paying.

options.label: Ignore it. Bad luck happens
options.outcome: You continue exactly as before, so the next client who shuts down can leave you ₹36,000 short again.
options.why: You may be right that nobody could have known the client would shut down. But you can still learn from the loss. It showed one thing you can control: when new clients pay you.
options.better: Ask new clients for the first month in advance.

screens.text: Win or lose, Dhoni's call was the same. Judge a call by what you ___ then, not by the ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Dhoni had to choose with what he knew then, and whether Misbah's scoop was caught or went for four couldn't change that choice afterwards. Judge your own calls the same way: first ask what you knew, then ask what the result can teach you.

summary: Judge a decision by what you knew when you made it.
A good bet can lose many times in a row, so don't drop it after one miss.
Don't let the result rewrite the old call, but use it to fix what you can next time.

cards.front: You checked everything, and the deal still failed. Was it a bad decision?
options: Not if the thinking was sound
cards.back: Judge what you knew then. A good call can have a bad result.

cards.front: A bet wins 1 time in 4. How often do you lose twice in a row?
cards.back: ¾ × ¾ = 9/16. Losing streaks are normal on good bets.
